qt: to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Laurent Castillo (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) Subject:

Matthieu Pigasse, president of the Combat press group and major shareholder in Mediawan, a large audiovisual production studio in Europe (producing TV series, films, documentaries, debate programmes and thematic TV channels), has stated that he wants to ‘exert as much influence as possible on the 2027 presidential election’ in order to defeat the National Rally1. Mr Pigasse and his French associates, Pierre-Antoine Capton and Xavier Niel, hold 50.01% of Mediawan's voting rights through their holding company TopCo Breteuil. However, Bpifrance, the French public investment bank, is part-financing the group’s acquisitions. Mediawan has also just acquired the US film and TV studio North Road2. 1.
Does this financing, granted by a public bank to an unambiguously leftist media group for the acquisition of new audiovisual media, comply with competition law?
Is this in compliance with the European Media Freedom Act3, which was drawn up to promote media pluralism and combat excessive concentration?

Will the Commission protect the integrity of the French presidential election from interference by leftist media and audiovisual empires, partly financed by public bodies controlled by the French Government?

at: (English version) to the Commission Catherine Griset (PfE), André Rougé (PfE), Laurent Castillo (PfE), Julie Rechagneux (PfE) (10 February 2026) Subject: Financing of leftist media and audiovisual empires by public banks Matthieu Pigasse, president of the Combat press group and major shareholder in Mediawan, a large audiovisual production studio in Europe (producing TV series, films, documentaries, debate programmes and thematic TV channels), has stated that he wants to ‘exert as much influence as possible on the 2027 presidential election’ in order to defeat the National Rally (1). Mr Pigasse and his French associates, Pierre-Antoine Capton and Xavier Niel, hold 50.01% of Mediawan's voting rights through their holding company TopCo Breteuil. However, Bpifrance, the French public investment bank, is part-financing the group’s acquisitions. Mediawan has also just acquired the US film and TV studio North Road (2). 1. Does this financing, granted by a public bank to an unambiguously leftist media group for the acquisition of new audiovisual media, comply with competition law? 2. Is this in compliance with the European Media Freedom Act (3), which was drawn up to promote media pluralism and combat excessive concentration? 3. Will the Commission protect the integrity of the French presidential election from interference by leftist media and audiovisual empires, partly financed by public bodies controlled by the French Government? Supporter (4) (13 April 2026) In accordance with EU law, a measure constitutes state aid if, cumulatively, (i) it is imputable to the State and financed through State resources, (ii) it confers a selective advantage to an undertaking, (iii) it is liable to affect trade between Member States and (iv) it distorts or threatens to distort competition. Financing granted by a State-owned investment bank, therefore, may not automatically constitute state aid. If a Member State intends to grant state aid, it is under an obligation to notify the measure to the Commission and obtain the Commission’s approval before the measure is implemented, unless the measure is covered by block exemptions. The European Media Freedom Act (1) does not prohibit investments or acquisitions in the media sector as such. It provides a framework for assessing media market concentrations that may affect media pluralism and editorial independence. National regulatory authorities and, where relevant, competition authorities remain responsible for the assessment of such transactions, in accordance with EU and national law. The European Media Board or the Commission may issue an opinion where the concentration is likely to affect the functioning of the internal market for media services. The conduct and the organisation of free and fair elections are the competence and responsibility of the Member States, in accordance with their national constitutional and legislative rules, while respecting their international obligations and EU law.
